industry.summary: Medical devices are a USD 650-680 bn global market growing ~5% a year, of which consumables and disposables are roughly a quarter; India is only ~2% of it (USD ~16 bn in 2025, per BCG/EY figures quoted by the company) but grows ~13% a year and imports 60-70% of what it uses. Polymed sells mostly low-cost, high-volume disposables (IV cannulae, infusion sets, blood bags, catheters) where scale, quality approvals and cost decide share, and is adding higher-value lines (dialysis, critical care, cardiology, orthopaedics) where clinical data and registrations take 2-3 years. About two-thirds of its sales are exports to 125+ countries, mainly to distributors and OEMs; the buyers are price-sensitive tenders and hospital groups, and the main rivals are multinationals (BD, B. Braun, Terumo, Nipro, Fresenius, Teleflex) and, increasingly, Chinese makers.
drivers: Hospital capacity and insurance: Indian hospitals moving from ~50% to 60-65% insured patients, which favours cheaper domestic devices (Q4FY26 call)
Import substitution: 60-70% of Indian device demand is imported; rupee weakness makes imports dearer
Ageing and chronic disease: dialysis, oncology ports, critical-care lines
Global sourcing shift to India (India-EU FTA, PLI scheme and medical-device parks; Q3FY26 PPT)
threats: Chinese dumping: dialysers enter India duty-free via ASEAN plants (anti-dumping probe opened on Polymed's application)
Price controls: coronary stents have been under NPPA price caps since 2017; tenders squeeze consumable prices
US tariffs (10% in Aug-2026) and a fluid trade policy
West-Asia war: shipping disruption (Middle East 6-8% of revenue)
Crude-linked resin and packaging costs (+~20% in early 2026)
industry.pricing: Pricing power is limited: Polymed took 3-5% price increases in Q1FY27 to pass on a ~20% rise in raw-material costs, and in renal it chose to raise prices and lose volume to Chinese imports rather than match them.

stockEvents: QIP of 53.19 lakh shares at ₹1,880 (₹1,000 cr); share count +5.5%
All-time high ₹3,129 (weekly close), ~95x the FY26 profit that followed
PendraCare and Citieffe acquisitions closed (~₹390 cr cash)
Q3FY26: profit −17%; IIFL downgrade to Reduce (₹1,230); stock ₹1,389
moat: Third-largest IV cannula maker globally (~11% share); 400+ moulding machines, 530+ automatic assembly lines, in-house tooling and sterilisation; gross margin ~68% standalone
EU MDR across all sites, 82 CE approvals, registrations in 100+ countries; only ~4 US FDA approvals of its own, so the US is barely open
15-20-year distributor and OEM relationships, 'hardly lost a large customer' (management); but buyers are price-driven and multi-source
399 patents, mostly incremental (safety cannulae, needle-free connectors); copycats exist
Cardiology (stents ₹10-12 cr), dialysis machines (~1,100 installed), orthopaedics via Citieffe: early, loss-making or low-margin
critiques: Growth has slowed: organic revenue grew only ~5% in FY26 (exports fell 3-4% ex-acquisitions) after 20%+ in FY23-25; FY27's +30% Q1 is mostly acquisitions.
The acquisitions dilute: PendraCare lost ₹14 cr before tax in its first six months and Citieffe's revenue was flat in CY25; consolidated EBITDA margin fell from 27.5% to 24.4%.

Working capital is heavy and rising: standalone cash conversion cycle 215 days (FY26) vs 183; receivables 98 days as Polymed gave customers longer terms; free cash flow was negative in FY23-26 on Screener's numbers.
The QIP cash is being used up: gross cash fell from ₹1,227 cr (Mar-25) to ₹842 cr (Mar-26) while debt rose to ₹342 cr; treasury income will fall.
Promoter pay is very high: MD, JMD and ED took ₹45 cr in FY26 (~10% of PBT; 497x the median employee for the MD).
The valuation history is extreme: the stock traded at 60-95x forward EPS in 2024 and at 25-40x in 2022-23; any median is sensitive to which years you include.
